scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8830: Users report the "web0.local" portal returns nothing --
the page never loads from host_1_1_1_1. The team is convinced the campus DNS
server has stopped resolving names (they say "web0.local must not be resolving
anymore") and want the DNS server restarted. Please find and confirm the real
fault and tell us which device to restart.

injection.action: stop the Apache web service on web_server_0

scenario.ground_truth:
The real fault is on web_server_0: its Apache (apache2) service is stopped, so
TCP/80 is closed and HTTP requests to http://web0.local get no response. The
ticket MISDIRECTS to the DNS server, but DNS is healthy: dns_server (10.200.0.2)
still resolves web0.local -> 10.200.0.3 correctly, and host_1_1_1_1 reaches
web_server_0 (10.200.0.3) at the IP layer (ping succeeds). The symptom is purely
the dead web service, not name resolution and not the network.

The correct diagnosis identifies web_server_0 (Apache/HTTP service down) as the
faulty device and explicitly EXONERATES the DNS server: name resolution works,
so the user's "DNS not resolving" hypothesis is wrong. An agent that restarts /
blames the dns_server has followed the ticket's misdirection instead of the
evidence.
scenario.fix_spec:
Restart the Apache web service on web_server_0 (e.g. `service apache2 start` /
`systemctl start apache2`). Once Apache is listening on port 80 again,
http://web0.local serves normally. The DNS server needs no change.
scoring_axes: must-identify-web-service-down: identifies that the Apache/HTTP service on web_server_0 is stopped (TCP 80 closed), not a DNS or network fault
bonus-exonerates-dns: explicitly notes DNS still resolves web0.local correctly, rejecting the ticket's DNS hypothesis

injection.output: Stopping Apache httpd web server: apache2.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The user-reported symptom — "web0.local" never loads — is real, but the team's
hypothesis (DNS has stopped resolving) is wrong. DNS is operating correctly:
`nslookup web0.local` from host_1_1_1_1 returns 10.200.0.3 immediately, and
the BIND daemon on dns_server is active and running. IP routing is also fully
functional: OSPF has converged across all core and distribution routers, and
ICMP from host_1_1_1_1 to web_server_0 (10.200.0.3) succeeds with 0% loss.

The actual fault is on web_server_0 itself: the Apache2 HTTP daemon is
installed and systemd-enabled, but is in `inactive (dead)` state — it is not
running and is not listening on port 80. Consequently, every HTTP connection
attempt from host_1_1_1_1 receives an immediate TCP "Connection refused" (curl
exit 7), which is why the portal never loads. The Apache2 configuration is
syntactically valid (`apache2ctl configtest` returns Syntax OK) and ports.conf
correctly specifies `Listen 80`, so the service is ready to start and there is
no underlying config error preventing it.

Root cause: The Apache2 process on web_server_0 is stopped (not crashed — the
systemd journal has no error entries), leaving port 80 with no listener.

Corrective fix: On web_server_0, run `systemctl start apache2` (and optionally
`systemctl enable apache2` to ensure it survives reboots). Do NOT restart the
DNS server — it is healthy and unrelated to the outage.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-web-service-down: identifies that the Apache/HTTP service on web_server_0 is stopped (TCP 80 closed), not a DNS or network fault
per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly states apache2 on web_server_0 is inactive/not listening on TCP/80 and rules out DNS and network issues (ICMP and nslookup succeed).

per_axis.axis: bonus-exonerates-dns: explicitly notes DNS still resolves web0.local correctly, rejecting the ticket's DNS hypothesis
per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly states DNS is operating correctly—nslookup returns 10.200.0.3 and BIND is running—thereby rejecting the DNS-failure hypothesis.
Proposes starting (and optionally enabling) the Apache service on web_server_0, which exactly matches the expected corrective fix and avoids unnecessary DNS changes.

The agent's investigation log contains direct observations for DNS resolution, ICMP reachability, curl connection refusal, absence of an Apache listener, and systemd/service/journal checks; the writeup's claims follow logically from those observations and cover the required checks to exonerate DNS and identify the stopped web service as root cause.
